headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: TREK handles secrets and user data while oh-my-openagent can ingest files, browse, and use MCP-like hooks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: oh-my-openagent can read local files and use runtime-injected MCPs/hooks, while TREK uses MCP and collaborative inputs. That creates a plausible instruction-injection path if TREK content is surfaced to A and then parsed as trusted text. The interaction is inferred from docs only, so uncertainty pushes to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF TREK content is passed into oh-my-openagent as file text or MCP output without provenance tags, injection is plausible.
IF either agent treats the other's generated text as instructions, prompt hijacking can occur.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated text into prompts.
Add provenance labels to all cross-agent messages.
Restrict MCP tools to allowlisted commands only.
Review any shared workspace for instruction-like content before reuse.
requires-engineering: add parser hardening and content-sanitization gates.

B_data_leakage.rationale: TREK touches reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets; oh-my-openagent touches session history, provider auth data, and project files, and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or hand off files, sensitive data can flow from B into A and then out to third parties. The blast radius includes secrets and account data, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF the two agents share files, logs, or copied prompts, TREK secrets can be exposed to oh-my-openagent.
IF oh-my-openagent forwards context to external services, leaked TREK data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and logs for each agent.
Remove secrets from any shared files before handoff.
Disable or restrict external network calls during cross-agent tasks.
Rotate any API keys or MFA secrets that may have been exposed.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can run browsers and use networked tools; A can spawn subprocesses and B can use MCP in a collaborative session. If they operate on the same mutable resources, they may race on shared files or remote state. No locking is documented, but the overlap is not enough to justify high because unrestricted same-dir writes are not explicitly shown.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or database, concurrent edits can conflict.
IF either agent mutates shared browser state or shared remote resources, last-write-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate directories and browser profiles.
Serialize writes to shared resources with a simple operator checklist.
Pause one agent before the other edits the same artifact.
Use read-only mode for one agent during review tasks.
requires-engineering: add explicit locking around shared mutable state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: TREK is a collaborative travel planner with AI built in, and oh-my-openagent can browse, call APIs, and use LSP/MCP-style tools. If A's output is fed into B without verification, B may act on incorrect travel facts or code-like instructions. The pathway exists in default-style workflows, but the harm is usually bounded to wrong plans rather than irreversible action.
conditions: IF TREK output is used as authoritative input to oh-my-openagent, downstream actions may be based on unverified facts.
IF oh-my-openagent executes browser or API actions from TREK-generated text, errors can cascade.
mitigations: Require a human review step before acting on peer output.
Cross-check key facts against source documents or live sites.
Mark peer-generated content as untrusted in prompts.
Limit automated actions to read-only verification passes.
requires-engineering: add confidence and provenance checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while oh-my-openagent handles provider auth data and session history with broad egress. That combination creates a likely compliance breach if travel PII or secrets are routed into A without a DPA/residency boundary. The profiles do not show matching controls, so uncertainty escalates to high.
conditions: IF EU PII or secrets from TREK are processed by oh-my-openagent without a documented DPA or residency control, compliance exposure exists.
IF retention or logging differs between the agents, the same data class may be retained inconsistently.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of cross-agent prompts.
Confirm residency and DPA terms before sharing any PII.
Disable verbose logging for sensitive workflows.
Purge shared logs after each task.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing and retention controls.
